Maintaining safety is a practice better accomplished through the use of effective safety measurement and monitoring. According to a framework for measurement published in a prominent safety journal, a lack of consensus about what is truly considered 'safe' can represent a significant hindrance when assessing whether a healthcare organization is safe. For example, safety can be considered a core set of standards, an attitude held by healthcare staff and leaders, or in terms of safety culture. Sometimes safety is associated with compliance and assurance, and other times it is approached through more active inquiry.
 
The findings of their report recommend asking five fundamental organizational safety questions when examining your safety measurement systems, in order to promote the useful discussion and adoption of solutions.
 
- Has patient care been safe in the past? We need to assess rates of past harm to patients, both physical and psychological.
 
- Are our clinical systems and processes reliable? This is the reliability of safety critical processes and systems but also the capacity of the staff to follow safety critical procedures.
 
- Is care safe today? This is the information and capacity to monitor safety on an hourly or daily basis. We refer to this as 'sensitivity to operations.'
 
- Will care be safe in the future? This refers to the ability to anticipate, and be prepared for, problems and threats to safety.
 
- Are we responding and improving? The capacity of an organization to detect, analyze, integrate, respond and improve from, safety information.
 
>Sources:

>Vincent C, Burnett S, Carthey J. BMJ Qual Saf Published Online First: [Retrieved 4 August 2020] doi:10.1136/bmjqs-2013-002757
